chapters.title: Chapter 4: Property, Unlisted Shares and Foreign Assets

lessons.title: Unlisted Shares, ESOP Shares and Startup Equity

body.text: Startup and ESOP shares are taxed in two stages: as salary when you get them, and as a capital gain when you sell. The value already taxed as salary becomes your cost. Miss that link and you pay tax twice on the same money.

children.text: Kavin, a 33-year-old product manager at a Bengaluru fintech startup, exercised his stock options in 2024. His employer deducted a large chunk of tax from his salary that month. In 2026, the company ran a secondary sale for employees, and Kavin sold his shares. When he filled in his capital gains, he used the ₹10 he had paid per share as his cost. His CA stopped him before he paid tax twice.

body.title: How Unlisted Share Taxation Has Changed

events.title: 20% with indexation
events.description: Long-term gains on unlisted shares for residents were taxed at 20% after indexing the cost for inflation.

events.title: 12.5% without indexation
events.description: The rate dropped to 12.5% but indexation was removed. Unlike property, there is no option to choose the old method for shares.

events.title: Angel tax abolished
events.description: The tax on startups receiving share premium above fair value was removed for investments from financial year 2025-26.

events.title: Buybacks become capital gains
events.description: Shareholders in both listed and unlisted companies are taxed on buyback proceeds as capital gains, not dividends.

body.title: Unlisted Share Clock
body.question: Rhea bought shares of a private Pune-based SaaS company from a founder in March 2025 and sells them to a new investor in September 2026. How is her gain taxed?
options: Long-term at 12.5% with the ₹1.25 lakh exemption
body.explanation: Unlisted shares need more than 24 months to become long-term. March 2025 to September 2026 is about 18 months, so the gain is short-term and taxed at her slab rate. The 20% rate and the ₹1.25 lakh exemption apply only to listed equity where STT is paid.

markDefs.definition: A right given by an employer to buy its shares at a fixed exercise price after a vesting period. Taxed as a salary perquisite on exercise and as a capital gain when the shares are sold.

children.text: goes through four stages. Only two of them trigger tax.

cells: The company promises you options at an exercise price
You earn the right to exercise after the vesting period
You pay the exercise price and shares are allotted to you
Perquisite taxed as salary at slab rate, usually with TDS by the employer
Capital gain, with cost equal to the FMV taxed at exercise

body.latex: \text{Perquisite} = (\text{FMV on exercise date} - \text{Exercise price}) \times \text{Shares}\\[6pt]\text{Capital gain} = \text{Sale value} - (\text{FMV on exercise date} \times \text{Shares})
body.caption: The FMV on the exercise date is the bridge: it caps the salary tax and becomes the starting cost for capital gains.

body.title: Kavin's Perquisite
body.prompt: Kavin exercised 2,000 options at an exercise price of ₹10. A merchant banker valued the shares at ₹310 on the exercise date. What perquisite value is added to his salary, in rupees?
body.explanation: Perquisite = (₹310 − ₹10) × 2,000 = ₹6,00,000. At his 30% slab, that is about ₹1,80,000 of tax before cess, deducted by his employer through payroll.

body.caption: Kavin sells all 2,000 shares in a secondary sale at ₹550, 30 months after allotment (illustrative)

body.label: The Double Tax Trap
body.context: Using the exercise price as cost would have overstated Kavin's gain by ₹6,00,000, the same amount already taxed as salary, and cost him ₹75,000 of avoidable capital gains tax before cess.

body.title: When Does the ESOP Clock Start?
body.textWithBlank: For capital gains, the holding period of ESOP shares starts from the date of ___ of the shares, not the grant or vesting date.
body.explanation: You only own the shares once they are allotted after exercise. Years of vesting before that do not count. Kavin's 30 months run from allotment, so his unlisted shares are long-term.

body.text: Employees of eligible startups get relief on the salary tax. If the startup has DPIIT recognition and an inter-ministerial board certificate for the startup tax holiday, tax on the ESOP perquisite can be deferred until the earliest of 48 months from the end of the relevant year of allotment, the date you sell the shares, or the date you leave the company. The perquisite value itself does not change; only the payment is postponed.

body.title: Deferred Tax Meets a Job Change
body.scenario: Divya works at a DPIIT-recognised startup with the required tax holiday certificate. She exercised options in 2025 and her employer deferred the perquisite tax. In October 2026, before the company has any liquidity event, she resigns to join another firm. She still holds the shares.
body.prompt: What happens to her deferred tax, and does resigning create a capital gain?
body.modelAnswer: Leaving the company is one of the three events that ends the deferral, so the deferred tax on her perquisite becomes payable soon after she resigns, and her former employer is required to deduct or collect it. Resigning is not a transfer of the shares, so no capital gain arises. She keeps the shares with a cost equal to the FMV on her exercise date, and a capital gain arises only when she eventually sells. This is why startup employees should plan for the cash to pay deferred tax before changing jobs, even if the shares are still illiquid.

children.text: Listed Employer Shares and Foreign RSUs

If your employer is listed in India, such as Infosys or HCLTech, the same two-stage logic applies. Once allotted, the shares are listed equity: long-term after more than 12 months, and gains on sale through the exchange are taxed at 20% or 12.5% with the ₹1.25 lakh exemption. ESOP allotments are not among the acquisitions excluded by the STT-on-purchase notification, so the concessional rates still apply. RSUs from a foreign parent such as Google or Microsoft are foreign shares, which Chapter 4, Lesson 3 covers.
Selling Unlisted Shares Below Fair Value

body.title: Selling Below Fair Market Value: Both Sides Are Exposed

columns.label: Seller
points: If you sell unlisted shares below their fair market value worked out under the Income-tax Rules, that fair market value is treated as your sale value
This rule was section 50CA of the 1961 Act and continues under the 2025 Act
Selling to a friend or relative at a "token" price can create a much larger taxable gain than the cash you received

columns.label: Buyer
points: If an individual buys unlisted shares for less than fair market value, the shortfall above ₹50,000 can be taxed as income from other sources
Gifts from relatives are an exception
Get a valuation report before any off-market deal in private company shares

children.text: Many investors now buy pre-IPO shares through unlisted share platforms. While the company is unlisted, those shares follow the 24-month clock and 12.5% long-term rate. Once the company lists, what matters is the nature of the shares when you sell. Shares sold on the exchange after listing are listed shares, so the 12-month threshold applies, and your holding period is generally counted from your original purchase date.

STT was not paid when you bought them, but that does not block section 198. The CBDT notification on the STT-on-purchase condition works by listing the kinds of acquisitions that do not qualify, and ordinary purchases made while a company was unlisted are not on that list. So if you hold for more than 12 months in total and sell on the exchange, the gain is generally taxed at 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh exemption.

content.text: Pre-IPO shareholders are usually subject to a SEBI lock-in after listing, so you may not be able to sell for several months. Factor that in before paying a high price on a platform.

(FMV on exercise − exercise price) × shares, taxed as salary at slab rate.
FMV on the exercise date, not the exercise price.
Starts on allotment of shares, not grant or vesting.
Perquisite tax postponed to the earliest of 48 months, sale or leaving, for eligible startups.
Sale below fair market value: fair market value becomes the seller's sale value.

body.title: Keep These Records for Every ESOP or Startup Holding
steps: Grant letter, vesting schedule and exercise confirmation showing exercise price
Allotment date and the merchant banker valuation or FMV used for the perquisite
Form 16 or payslip showing the perquisite value and TDS, or deferral details
Share certificates or demat statement showing when the shares were credited
Sale agreement, secondary sale confirmation or buyback letter with price and date
A valuation report for any off-market sale or purchase of unlisted shares

points: Unlisted shares are long-term after more than 24 months and taxed at 12.5% without indexation or the ₹1.25 lakh exemption
ESOPs are taxed as salary on exercise and as capital gains on sale
Your capital gains cost is the FMV on the exercise date, not the exercise price you paid
The holding period for ESOP shares starts on allotment
Eligible startup employees can defer perquisite tax, but the deferral ends on sale, leaving or 48 months
Selling unlisted shares below fair market value can make that fair value your taxable sale price

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or investment advice. Company names are used only as examples, and share values, prices and option numbers are illustrative. Sections and rates reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 for tax year 2026-27. ESOP and startup equity outcomes depend on plan documents and valuations, so consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
